newsitem.title: USA: Ex-welder, priest, scientist win U.S. book awards.
newsitem.headline: Ex-welder, priest, scientist win U.S. book awards.

text.p: Writers who began work in diverse fields -- welding, the priesthood, zoology -- won three of the four U.S. National Book Awards on Wednesday.
Andrea Barrett won the award for fiction with her book, "Ship Fever and Other Stories," a collection of short stories that focuses on science and human behaviour.

The title story "Ship Fever" deals with Irish immigrants who fled the potato famine only to die of typhus, then known as Ship Fever, contracted because of the squalor on the holding islands for Canadian immigrants.

Barrett, who studied biology as an undergraduate, then zoology, briefly, as a graduate student, said she did not understand at the time that she did not have the mind of a scientist. But, she said, in her stories she found a way to use her love of science.
"An American Requiem: God, My Father, and the War that Came Between Us" won the non-fiction award for James Carroll, a Boston Globe columnist who was a Catholic priest during the Vietnam War.
"Well, perhaps now the first sentence of my obituary won't refer to my being an ex-priest," he said while accepting the award at a ceremony at the Waldorf-Astoria Hotel.
For the first time in the 46 year history of the awards, the National Book Federation honoured young people's literature.
Victor Martinez won the young people's literature award for "Parrot in the Oven: Mi Vida," the story of an Hispanic boy in his early teens living in public housing.
Martinez said he especially wanted to reach out to teens because at that age many Chicano people ruined their lives by joining gangs, selling drugs or taking menial work.
"I was trained to be a welder," he said. "A counsellor called me in and said 'You know, you're a very smart boy. You should be a welder.' It was because I was Mexican," he said.
Hayden Carruth won the National Book Award for Poetry for "Scrambled Eggs and Whisky." Carruth, who has published more than 20 books, did not attend the ceremony because he was ill.
When the pool of nominees was announced in October they evoked some controversy because several successful and widely acclaimed works had been left out in favour of more obscure writers.
As previously announced, novelist Toni Morrison won the National Book Foundation Medal for Distinguished Contribution to American Letters.

She urged the winners and nominees to "not spend one second" worrying about the controversy, but instead to enjoy the honour as a "fleeting but at the same time permanent acknowledgment" of their talent.
